subject: history
displayName: KS3 History — Migration to Britain Through Time
subtitle: How waves of migration — from Romans to Windrush — shaped Britain's culture, society, and identity.

data.targetWord: the movement of people from one place to another to live for a period of time or permanently

examples.en-GB: Migration has shaped Britain since ancient times, from Roman soldiers to Commonwealth workers.

data.targetWord: a reason that encourages or forces someone to leave a place, such as war, poverty or persecution

examples.en-GB: The Great Famine was a push factor that caused mass Irish migration to Britain in the 1840s.

data.targetWord: a reason that attracts someone to a place, such as work, safety, family or education

examples.en-GB: Jobs in the NHS and on the railways were pull factors that attracted Windrush migrants to Britain.

data.targetWord: a person forced to leave their country because of danger, such as war, persecution or serious threat

examples.en-GB: Huguenots were refugees who fled religious persecution in France after 1685.

data.targetWord: unfair or cruel treatment of people because of their identity, religion, ethnicity, politics or beliefs

examples.en-GB: Jewish people in medieval England faced persecution, heavy taxation, false accusations, and ultimately expulsion in 1290.

data.targetWord: a community of people who live outside their original homeland but keep cultural, family or historical links with it

examples.en-GB: The Caribbean diaspora in Britain maintained strong cultural and family connections with their home islands.

data.targetWord: the process by which people become part of a society while often keeping parts of their own culture and identity

examples.en-GB: Over generations, many Huguenot families integrated into British society while maintaining their Protestant faith.

data.targetWord: treating people unfairly because of characteristics such as race, religion, nationality, language, gender or background

examples.en-GB: Windrush generation migrants often faced discrimination in housing and employment despite their essential contributions.

data.targetWord: a voluntary association of countries, many of which were once part of the British Empire, maintaining political and cultural links

examples.en-GB: After 1948, people from Commonwealth countries had legal rights to settle in Britain as British subjects.

data.targetWord: the act of forcing a person or group to leave a country or area by government or royal order

examples.en-GB: In 1290 King Edward I ordered the expulsion of Jewish people from England, the first such order in medieval Europe.

data.targetWord: Germanic peoples from northern Europe (Angles, Saxons, Jutes) who settled in Britain from around the 400s-600s, influencing language and place names

examples.en-GB: Anglo-Saxon settlement gave England many place names ending in -ham, -ton and -ing.

data.targetWord: the area of northern and eastern England where Danish Viking influence and law was strongest in the ninth and tenth centuries

examples.en-GB: Place names ending in -by and -thorpe in the Danelaw area show the extent of Viking settlement.

data.targetWord: the successful invasion of England by William, Duke of Normandy, in 1066, which changed landownership, government and language

examples.en-GB: The Norman Conquest brought French words into English and changed who owned the land through the Domesday Book.

data.targetWord: French Protestants who fled religious persecution in France, especially after the revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685

examples.en-GB: Huguenot refugees brought skills in silk weaving, clockmaking and banking when they settled in England after 1685.

data.targetWord: Caribbean migrants who came to Britain after World War Two, named after the HMT Empire Windrush which arrived at Tilbury in June 1948

examples.en-GB: The Windrush generation helped rebuild post-war Britain by working in the NHS, on buses and in factories.

data.targetWord: the programme in 1938-1939 that brought approximately 10,000 mostly Jewish children from Nazi-controlled Europe to Britain

examples.en-GB: Children who arrived on the Kindertransport were placed with British families or in hostels to escape Nazi persecution.

data.targetWord: an African writer and anti-slavery campaigner who lived in eighteenth-century Britain and helped persuade people to oppose the slave trade

examples.en-GB: Olaudah Equiano's autobiography was used to show the cruelty of slavery and supported the abolitionist movement.

data.targetWord: the 1972 order by Ugandan ruler Idi Amin for Asians to leave Uganda, after which many settled in Britain and rebuilt their lives

examples.en-GB: Many Ugandan Asians expelled in 1972 settled in Leicester and other British cities, becoming important parts of those communities.

data.targetWord: a person who has asked another country for protection as a refugee and is waiting for a decision on their claim

examples.en-GB: The distinction between a refugee and an asylum seeker is that the asylum seeker is still waiting for their claim to be decided.

data.targetWord: the variety within a society, including different cultures, languages, religions, traditions and backgrounds

examples.en-GB: Migration has created remarkable diversity in British cities, with communities from every part of the world.

data.targetWord: the act of living in a place for a long period, often involving forming communities, workplaces and places of worship

examples.en-GB: Huguenot settlement in London's East End left a lasting mark on local industry and religious life.

data.targetWord: the Roman settlement founded after the conquest of 43 CE that became the major city now known as London

examples.en-GB: Londinium was a multicultural Roman city, home to soldiers and traders from across the empire.

data.targetWord: evidence based on the spoken memories and testimonies of people who experienced historical events, often recorded in interviews

examples.en-GB: Oral history interviews with Windrush migrants reveal personal experiences of both opportunity and discrimination.

data.targetWord: the catastrophe in Ireland in the 1840s when potato blight and government failures caused mass starvation and death, driving large-scale emigration

examples.en-GB: The Great Famine of the 1840s caused over a million deaths in Ireland and pushed many more to migrate to Britain and America.

data.targetWord: the 1685 decision by King Louis XIV of France to cancel the protection previously granted to French Protestants, causing Huguenot refugees to flee

examples.en-GB: When Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes in 1685, thousands of Huguenots fled to England, the Dutch Republic and Prussia.

data.sentence: A reason that forces someone to leave a place, such as war or poverty, is called a ____ factor.
A person forced to leave their country because of danger or persecution is called a ____.
The Roman conquest of Britain began in ____ CE.
King Edward I ordered the ____ of Jewish people from England in 1290.
Huguenots were French ____ who fled persecution after 1685.
HMT Empire Windrush arrived at Tilbury in Essex in ____, becoming a symbol of post-war Caribbean migration.
The ____ campaign in 1938-1939 brought Jewish and other children from Nazi-controlled Europe to safety in Britain.
Huguenots contributed skills in silk weaving, ____, and banking to English society.
Irish migrants in the nineteenth century often worked building ____, canals and docks in industrial Britain.
A community living outside its original homeland but keeping links to it is called a ____.
Ugandan Asians were expelled from Uganda by ____ in 1972.
The Irish ____ of the 1840s, caused by potato blight, was a major push factor for migration to Britain.
Viking place names ending in ____ and -thorpe can still be found in northern and eastern England.
The anti-slavery campaigner ____ used his autobiography to persuade people to oppose the slave trade.
When people arrive in a new country and ask for protection while their claim is being decided, they are called ____ seekers.
The Norman Conquest of 1066 was led by William, Duke of ____, who brought major changes to England's government and language.
Windrush migrants often worked in the NHS, on public transport, and in ____, contributing to Britain's post-war recovery.

data.title: Put these migration events in chronological order
items: Roman conquest begins — soldiers and traders arrive from across the empire (43 CE)
Anglo-Saxon settlement — groups from northern Europe settle in Britain (400s-600s)
Viking raids and settlement — Scandinavians settle in northern and eastern England (790s-1000s)
Norman Conquest — William of Normandy changes England's ruling class (1066)
Expulsion of Jewish people from England by Edward I (1290)
Huguenot refugees flee to England after revocation of Edict of Nantes (1685)

data.title: Order these modern migration events from earliest to most recent
items: Irish migration increases due to the Great Famine (1840s)
Jewish refugees flee persecution in Eastern Europe, settling in London's East End (1880s-1900s)
Kindertransport brings Jewish children from Nazi Europe to Britain (1938-1939)
HMT Empire Windrush arrives at Tilbury — symbol of Caribbean migration (1948)
Ugandan Asians expelled by Idi Amin settle in Britain (1972)

data.title: Order the cause-and-consequence chain for Huguenot migration
items: Louis XIV issues decree of religious intolerance in France
Edict of Nantes is revoked in 1685, ending Protestant protections
Thousands of Huguenots flee France fearing persecution
Huguenots settle in England, especially London and Canterbury
Huguenots contribute silk weaving, clockmaking and banking skills
Some British workers initially fear competition from newcomers

pairs.text: Work available in the NHS and on buses
The Great Famine causing mass starvation in Ireland
Family members already settled in Britain
Irish workers building railways in industrial Britain
Flemish weavers in the cloth trade
Jewish refugees from Eastern European pogroms
